newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi says open to some change on Euro-tax.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi says open to some change on Euro-tax.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Thursday it was possible to modify a "Euro-tax" designed to help Italy join a European currency union at the start, but the overall thrust of the package must remain unchanged.
"The Euro-tax will be discussed first in commission and then in the Senate (upper house)," Prodi told reporters at a news conference after a cabinet meeting.

"Variations and improvements are certainly possible but the overall framework cannot be changed because it is part of the strategy of adhering to the Maastricht criteria and overhauling Italian public finances," he said.
The Maastricht criteria set tough economic targets for European Union states to meet in order to qualify for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) planned for launch in 1999.
The government late on Wednesday bowed to widespread criticism and announced changes to the planned one-off levy, which is designed to raise 12.5 trillion lire ($8.3 billion).
The small centrist party of Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, which belongs to Prodi's coalition, unveiled alternatives to the Euro-tax that it said would spread the sacrifices more fairly.
But Massimo D'Alema, whose Democratic Party of the Left is the biggest party in government, rejected Dini's move, saying it unacceptably altered the balance of the Euro-tax.

Government undersecretary Enrico Micheli said the government was still open to suggestions from all sides on the tax, which is due to be levied next year. "Ours is not a closed proposal but the revenue must stay the same," he said.
Parliamentary party and commission leaders in the Senate were due to meet at 1730 GMT to discuss amendments to the budget which have been submitted.
The 1997 budget aims to chop 62.5 trillion lire off next year's deficit.
